title: The Zero Paradox: A Multi-Framework Mathematical Ontology
description: A formal mathematical framework proving the Binary Snap - the forced transition from the bottom element ⊥ to the minimum nonzero state ε₀ - as a theorem across lattice algebra, p-adic topology, information theory, functional analysis, and category theory. The central result is derived from the standard bottom-element axiom of join-semilattice theory, without snap-specific axioms, and verified sorry-free in Lean 4 + Mathlib; the central theorem is machine-verified to depend on no axioms at all, with Classical.choice appearing only in the layers that realize the snap inside standard analytic structures (inherited from Mathlib, its necessity there open). The formal layers included, each verified sorry-free in Lean 4 + Mathlib, are: ZP-A (lattice algebra), ZP-B (p-adic topology), ZP-C (information theory), ZP-D (functional analysis / state layer), ZP-E (cross-framework synthesis / T-SNAP derivation), ZP-F (counterexamples - the snap fails in all ordered fields), ZP-G (category theory), ZP-H (categorical bridge, with the snap floor realized as genuine functors into the real Mathlib categories TopCat, ModuleCat ℂ, and the Kleisli category of the probability monad), ZP-I (inside zero), ZP-J (self-reference / AFA decoration uniqueness / wheel of fractions - division by zero as a total operation), ZP-K (computational grounding), ZP-L (incomputability convergence / ε₀ as ordinal snap threshold), ZP-M (Kleene-ordinal bridge), ZP-N (the constructive snap - the ε₀ snap rebuilt syntactically from below on ordinal notations, choice-free, showing ZP-L's Classical.choice at ε₀ to be representational rather than intrinsic), ZP-P (the fixed-point fork - a synthesis layer: least versus greatest fixed point, i.e. induction / well-founded versus coinduction / non-well-founded closure, with a choice-free Knaster–Tarski fork schema and the diagonal fixed point ⊥ at the collapse seam, where choice enters only the non-well-founded realizations and is inherited from Mathlib), and ZP-Q (the frame-change - ⊥→ε₀ as a change of point of view: the order-theoretic frame-flip universal holds, valuation and categorical per-domain instances are built, and the categorical Lawvere universal meets a proven Cantor wall, with the cross-domain identity a type boundary), and ZP-R (cross-category fixed point - a synthesis / placement layer locating and realizing the self-application fixed point ⊥ as a Lawvere fixed point across three faces: refuted in Set (Cantor), a fork rather than a reflexive object in the monotone / domain regime, and realized in the computability face, with existence, uniqueness, and location each proved but face-local and the global cross-category identification held as a fenced conjecture; its Diagonal Family Addendum records the complete diagonal-family roster tied to ⊥ by the μ/ν fork - wall faces such as Cantor, Russell, Turing, Tarski, and Curry where self-reference cannot close, and floor faces such as the Quine atom, the Kleene quine, Löb / Gödel-2, and Rice where it closes and lands at ⊥ - with the unification credited to Lawvere (1969) and Yanofsky (2003) and the contribution the axiom-free core formalization and the tie to ⊥). The framework's claims are mapped against established prior art in a 'Convergence with established work' ledger (CLAIMS.md), with credit pointing outward and an honest delta for each, and the claim graph itself is machine-checked (ClaimsMirror.lean), each proved status a verified link to a green Lean declaration rather than a label; and a ZP-J Keystone Addendum records two machine-checked investigations of the keystone (the self-referential 'diagonal' fixed point at the floor): a face-by-face Lawvere verdict, and the binary snap as a crossing of the well-foundedness boundary (Taylor; Adámek-Milius-Moss), with the full coalgebraic version flagged open.
